query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy, the introduction of a modest amount (~5 at%) of molybdenum combined with an optimized high‐temperature aging treatment will induce the formation of fine, uniformly distributed precipitates that obstruct dislocation motion, thereby enhancing the alloy’s elevated‐temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the as-cast, unmodified material.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with elements in the 5–35 at% range forming a uniform solid solution without intentional precipitate-forming additions.
generation.intervention: Addition of approximately 5 atomic percent molybdenum followed by a controlled aging heat treatment (e.g., heating at ~1050°C for 2 hours) designed to promote the nucleation and growth of fine precipitates.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied to the alloy within its compositional window (each constituent at 5–35 at%) and is evaluated during high-temperature mechanical testing at temperatures around 1200°C; care is taken to avoid excessive refractory phase formation that could embrittle the alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine-scale precipitate phase (e.g., intermetallic or sigma phase) dispersed in the homogeneous solid solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitates produced by the molybdenum addition and heat treatment will hinder dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby raising the yield strength and improving creep resistance at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to show a significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (on the order of roughly 10–20% improvement) compared to the baseline alloy, though precise improvement levels require further quantification.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy produced without additional molybdenum and without the post-synthesis aging heat treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable within the compositional limits of high-entropy alloys (each element between 5 and 35 at%) and for operating temperatures in the high-temperature regime (approximately 1200°C to 1600°C); excessive Mo content or inappropriate heat-treatment parameters may lead to coarse or brittle precipitates, negating the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: The exact precipitate phases, their morphology, and the quantitative improvement in strength depend on the detailed alloy processing conditions and require careful microstructural characterization and mechanical testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the titanium- and nickel-primary HEA: one set with a 5 at% molybdenum addition followed by an aging heat treatment (e.g., 1050°C for 2 hours), and a control set produced without Mo addition and heat treatment. Subject both sets to high-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., yield and creep testing at ~1200°C) and perform microstructural analysis (using TEM and XRD) to assess precipitate formation.
measurements: Elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance
Precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added, aged samples show no statistically significant increase (e.g., less than a 10% improvement) in yield strength or creep resistance at elevated temperatures or if microstructural analysis does not reveal the formation of fine, uniformly distributed precipitates compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. AbstractSingle-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been receiving significant attention due to their excellent mechanical properties and phase stability at elevated temperatures. Recently, many studies have been reported regarding the precipitation-enhanced alloy design strategy to further improve the mechanical properties of RHEAs at elevated temperatures. In this study, we attempted to develop precipitation-hardened light-weight RHEAs via addition of Ni or Co into Al0.8NbTiV HEA. The added elements were selected due to their smaller atomic radius and larger mixing enthalpy, which is known to stimulate the formation of precipitates. The addition of the Ni or Co leads to the formation of the sigma precipitates with homogeneous distribution. The formation and homogeneous distribution of sigma particles plays a critical role in improvement of yield strength. Furthermore, the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) HEAs show excellent specific yield strength compared to single-phase AlNbTiV and NbTiVZr RHEA alloys and conventional Ni-based superalloy (Inconel 718) at elevated temperatures.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory alloys, lightweight, sigma phase, mech

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as alloys that are composed of more than 4 elements with near equi-atomic percentage [,,,]. Due to their high mixing entropy, HEAs tend to form simple solid-solution phases, such as face-centered-cubic (FCC) [,], body-centered-cubic (BCC) [,,], and hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) structures [,]. With the entropic stabilization of solid-solution phases, HEAs have attracted significant attention, because of their outstanding properties at elevated temperatures, which results from severe lattice distortion and microstructural stability at high temperatures [,,]. Many refractory HEAs (RHEAs), which mainly consist of BCC-type single solid-solution phase, have been developed and investigated due to their excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures []. The excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures in RHEAs are significantly associated with their unique atomic structures (distorted lattices) and high melting temperatures of the constitutive refractory elements (Ti, Nb, V, Mo, Ta, W, and Cr) [,,,].
